objectives: Use fever duration and prior treatment history to avoid blind malaria retreatment.
Broaden differential diagnosis in prolonged fever with abdominal symptoms.
Select evidence-based outpatient or referral plan based on danger signs and trend.
takeaways: Fever lasting over one week after prior AL should trigger reassessment, not repeat malaria therapy.
Abdominal symptoms and persistent fever require focused exam and targeted investigations.
Safety-net counseling is essential because prolonged fever can evolve quickly.
learnCaseOverrides.blurb: A man with more than a week of fever and abdominal symptoms already took antimalarials without improvement. Decide how to reassess before treating again.

sections.title: Chief complaint
sections.text: Fever for 9 days with abdominal discomfort and poor appetite

sections.title: Medication history
sections.text: Completed artemether-lumefantrine from drug shop 4 days ago with no improvement.

coach.title: Paul has unresolved fever
coach.body: He is tired but alert. Your key challenge is resisting reflex retreatment for malaria.
coach.quote: “I finished malaria medicine, but fever never really went away.”

teach.label: Clinical framing
teach.text: Duration and treatment response are powerful clues; prolonged fever should widen your diagnostic lens.

sections.title: Danger-sign check
sections.reveal_note: No immediate referral danger signs identified.

coach.title: What is the best next move?
coach.body: He is stable now, but fever has persisted despite prior antimalarial treatment.

options.text: Perform focused prolonged-fever assessment and broaden differential diagnosis before prescribing
Repeat artemether-lumefantrine immediately because fever is still present
Give steroids and observe response before taking history
Discharge with antipyretics only and no follow-up plan

question.right: Correct. Fever for 9 days after prior AL should trigger structured reassessment. Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023 supports test-guided management rather than blind retreatment.
question.wrong: This chart already shows treatment failure to prior AL. Repeating malaria therapy without reassessment risks delaying diagnosis of other febrile illnesses.

sections.title: Focused exam findings
sections.result_value: Diffuse abdominal tenderness, no guarding, mild dehydration

coach.title: What does this pattern suggest?
coach.body: You now have prolonged fever, negative RDT, and abdominal findings.

question.prompt: Which management path is most appropriate now?

options.text: Treat as probable non-malarial prolonged febrile illness per guideline, hydrate, and arrange close review/referral triggers
Ignore negative RDT and restart full malaria treatment
Prescribe multiple unrelated medicines without documenting diagnosis
Avoid treatment and tell patient prolonged fever is expected

question.right: Correct. Negative RDT plus persistent abdominal fever features support a broadened non-malarial working diagnosis and targeted management with close follow-up.
question.wrong: The chart points away from uncomplicated malaria. Repeating AL blindly misses the prolonged-fever assessment this patient needs.

sections.title: Outpatient plan
sections.drug: Targeted prolonged-fever treatment per local protocol
sections.detail: Hydration + symptom control + specific therapy based on working diagnosis

coach.title: What follow-up advice is safest?
coach.body: Persistent fever needs a clear return plan.

question.prompt: Which counseling should accompany this plan?

options.text: Give strict return precautions for persistent fever, confusion, vomiting, or worsening abdominal pain within 24-48 hours
Tell him to return only after one full week regardless of symptoms
Advise buying more antimalarials if fever spikes again
Skip counseling because he has had fever for many days already

question.right: Correct. Prolonged fever can worsen quickly; explicit danger-sign return advice is essential to safe outpatient management.
question.wrong: This case needs active follow-up planning. Delayed or vague review advice increases risk of missed deterioration.

sections.title: Case outcome
sections.text: You avoided blind malaria retreatment and used prolonged-fever logic to guide management.
sections.emphasis: Duration, treatment history, and test results changed the plan.

coach.title: Key teaching points
coach.body: Paul's >1 week fever and no response to prior AL were red flags for anchoring bias. By integrating negative malaria testing, abdominal findings, and safety-net follow-up, you applied Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023 principles for rational febrile illness care.

teach.label: Clinician review
teach.text: When fever persists despite prior treatment, pause and reframe the case before prescribing again.
